topic_tag: hiking time estimate from a map scale and a climbing allowance
subskill: converting a map length with a ratio scale, converting decimal hours to minutes, and adding a per-100-meter allowance for climbs only across a route with two ascents
prompt: A hiking guidebook estimates the time needed for a route with this rule: walking time at 4 kilometers per hour over the route's horizontal length, plus 10 minutes for every 100 meters of climbing. Descending adds no time. On a map with a scale of 1:25,000, a certain route measures 39.2 centimeters. The route starts at a trailhead at an elevation of 368 meters, climbs steadily to a summit at 1,146 meters, descends to a saddle at 861 meters, climbs to a second summit at 1,043 meters, and then descends to its finish at 486 meters. To the nearest minute, what is the guidebook's estimated time for the route, in minutes?
explanation: On the map, 39.2 cm represents 39.2 × 25,000 = 980,000 cm = 9.8 km. At 4 km/h, walking takes 9.8 ÷ 4 = 2.45 hours = 2.45 × 60 = 147 minutes. The route climbs 1,146 − 368 = 778 m to the first summit and 1,043 − 861 = 182 m from the saddle to the second summit, 960 m in all, which adds 960 ÷ 100 × 10 = 96 minutes. The estimate is 147 + 96 = 243 minutes. The option "261" reads 2.45 hours as 2 hours 45 minutes (165 minutes). The option "292" measures the second climb from the trailhead (1,043 − 368 = 675 m) instead of from the saddle. The option "299" also charges the final 557-meter descent as if it were climbing.
solve: const km=39.2*25000/100000; const walk=km/4*60; const climb=(1146-368)+(1043-861); return String(Math.round(walk+climb/10));

distractor_solve.261: const km=39.2*25000/100000; const h=km/4; const misread=Math.floor(h)*60+Math.round((h%1)*100); const climb=(1146-368)+(1043-861); return String(Math.round(misread+climb/10));
distractor_solve.292: const km=39.2*25000/100000; const walk=km/4*60; const climb=(1146-368)+(1043-368); return String(Math.round(walk+climb/10));
distractor_solve.299: const km=39.2*25000/100000; const walk=km/4*60; const climb=(1146-368)+(1043-861)+(1043-486); return String(Math.round(walk+climb/10));

distractor_kind.261: decimal hours read as hours:minutes (2.45 h -> 2 h 45 min). (a) limiting case: no parameter extreme; walking time is fixed by the map. (b) neighbouring setup: not an adjacent problem, a unit slip; 261 is not an endpoint of any interval. (c) cheapest one-step bracket over the whole time: floor = walk + (highest point - start)/10 = 147 + 77.8 = 224.8 (total climb is at least the rise to the highest point); ceiling = walk + all vertical change/10 = 147 + (960 + 285 + 557)/10 = 327.2. 261 strictly inside. (d) real: the classic decimal-time slip.
distractor_kind.292: second climb measured from the trailhead elevation instead of the saddle. (a) no. (b) neighbouring setup (climb counted from the start each time) gives 292.3; inside (224.8, 327.2), not on either end. (c) strictly inside. (d) real: using the starting elevation as the reference for every summit.
distractor_kind.299: the last descent (1,043 -> 486) charged as climbing. (a) no. (b) charging ALL descents would sit ON the 327.2 ceiling, which is why that version is not used; charging one descent is 298.7, strictly inside. (c) strictly inside (224.8, 327.2). (d) real: ignoring the rule that descents add nothing for one leg of the route.

bounds: v > 147 + (1146-368)/10 = 224.8 (climb at least the rise to the highest point)
arith_class_check: No. All four options are 3-digit integers, none a multiple of 10 or 5; the stem forces an integer (nearest minute) on every option alike, and the gaps (18, 31, 7) are not a run.
one_sided_check: Key smallest, three different error kinds (a time-format slip, a wrong reference elevation, a descent charged as climb). The stem does not reveal a direction: the natural under-counts (net change only, first climb only) exist and lead below the key, and the decimal-hours slip direction is not visible without computing 2.45 h.
interior_parity_check: Interior options 261 and 292: both 3-digit integers, neither a multiple of 5 or 10, equal display complexity; the key 243 is an extreme, not interior.

topic_tag: handicap index from the lowest two of three slope-adjusted differentials
subskill: computing three rate-adjusted values from a given formula, selecting the two lowest computed values (not the two lowest raw scores), and averaging them
prompt:
A golfer's handicap differential for one round is found with the formula (score − course rating) × 113 ÷ slope rating. Her handicap index is the average of the two LOWEST differentials from her three most recent rounds. Her three most recent rounds are shown below.

Round 1: score 87, course rating 70.1, slope rating 119
Round 2: score 93, course rating 75.6, slope rating 144
Round 3: score 90, course rating 71.8, slope rating 131

To the nearest hundredth, what is her handicap index?
explanation: The differentials are (87 − 70.1) × 113 ÷ 119 ≈ 16.048 for round 1, (93 − 75.6) × 113 ÷ 144 ≈ 13.654 for round 2, and (90 − 71.8) × 113 ÷ 131 ≈ 15.699 for round 3. The two lowest are 13.654 and 15.699, so the index is (13.654 + 15.699) ÷ 2 ≈ 14.68. The option "15.13" averages all three differentials. The option "15.87" averages the differentials of the two lowest SCORES (rounds 1 and 3) instead of the two lowest differentials. The option "17.15" averages the two lowest values of score − course rating without the 113 ÷ slope adjustment.
quantity_asked: handicap index = mean of the two smallest of (s - r)*113/slope over the three rounds = (13.654 + 15.699)/2.

distractor_kind.15.13: averages all three differentials. (a) no limiting case. (b) neighbouring setup (average of all rounds); not an interval endpoint: the index can be anywhere between the smallest and largest differential. (c) cheapest bracket: the index lies between the smallest and largest differential, (13.65, 16.05); strictly inside. (d) real: ignoring the "two lowest" selection rule.
distractor_kind.15.87: selects by lowest score instead of lowest differential. (a) no. (b) a different selection, strictly inside (13.65, 16.05). (c) inside. (d) real: the round with the highest score has the lowest differential here because its course is hardest; picking by score is the natural mistake.
distractor_kind.17.15: drops the 113/slope adjustment. (a) no. (b) best two unadjusted differences (16.9 and 17.4) average 17.15; it is not the endpoint of any stem-forced interval. (c) cheapest bracket that does not require computing the factor: the index is (s - r) scaled by 113/slope with slopes 119 to 144, so between 0.78 and 0.95 of the raw differences, about (13.2, 17.3); 17.15 strictly inside. Rejecting it needs the factor applied, which is the item's own work. (d) real: forgetting the slope term.

arith_class_check: No. Four 2-decimal values with nonzero last digits; the index is the mean of two irrational-looking quotients, so no stem-readable divisibility or integrality applies to any option.
one_sided_check: Key smallest; three different error kinds (no selection, selection by score, missing slope factor). A student cannot see from the stem that selection by score raises the index: it does so only because the highest score is on the hardest course, which needs the differentials computed. The missing-factor direction also needs the factor computed.
interior_parity_check: Interior options 15.13 and 15.87: both 2-decimal values with nonzero hundredths, 4 significant digits, equal display complexity; key 14.68 is the smallest, not interior.

topic_tag: credit-weighted grade point average with a retaken course replacing the first attempt
subskill: weighting grade points by credit hours and applying a replacement policy so the retaken course counts once, with the retake grade
prompt:
At a college, a student's grade point average (GPA) is the total of (credit hours × grade points) for the courses counted, divided by the total credit hours counted, where an A is worth 4 grade points, a B is worth 3, a C is worth 2, and a D is worth 1. When a course is retaken, only the retake is counted: the first attempt's grade and credit hours are dropped. Lena's courses are listed below.

Calculus, 5 credit hours: A
Chemistry, 4 credit hours: D on the first attempt; B on the retake
Literature, 4 credit hours: B
Physics, 5 credit hours: A
Spanish, 3 credit hours: C
Economics, 3 credit hours: B

To the nearest hundredth, what is Lena's GPA?
explanation: Counting Chemistry once, with the B, the grade points are 5(4) + 4(3) + 4(3) + 5(4) + 3(2) + 3(3) = 20 + 12 + 12 + 20 + 6 + 9 = 79 over 5 + 4 + 4 + 5 + 3 + 3 = 24 credit hours, so the GPA is 79 ÷ 24 ≈ 3.29. The option "2.96" also counts the first Chemistry attempt, adding 4 credit hours of D: 83 ÷ 28. The option "3.17" averages the six letter grades without weighting by credit hours: 19 ÷ 6. The option "3.25" keeps the 4 credit hours of both attempts but gives both the retake's B: 91 ÷ 28.
solve: const cr=[5,4,4,5,3,3], g=[4,3,3,4,2,3]; let P=0,C=0; cr.forEach((c,i)=>{P+=c*g[i];C+=c;}); return (Math.round(P/C*100+1e-9)/100).toFixed(2);

distractor_solve.2.96: const cr=[5,4,4,5,3,3], g=[4,3,3,4,2,3]; let P=4*1,C=4; cr.forEach((c,i)=>{P+=c*g[i];C+=c;}); return (Math.round(P/C*100+1e-9)/100).toFixed(2);
distractor_solve.3.25: const cr=[5,4,4,5,3,3], g=[4,3,3,4,2,3]; let P=4*3,C=4; cr.forEach((c,i)=>{P+=c*g[i];C+=c;}); return (Math.round(P/C*100+1e-9)/100).toFixed(2);

quantity_asked: GPA = 79/24 with Chemistry counted once at B.

distractor_kind.2.96: first attempt not dropped (D kept as an extra 4-credit course). (a) no. (b) neighbouring setup (no replacement policy) = 83/28 = 2.96; the feasible range of a GPA built from these grades is (2, 4); strictly inside. (c) cheapest bracket: between the lowest and highest grade counted, (2, 4); inside. Lattice: 2.96 rounds from 71/24, so a k/24 integrality test does not reject it. (d) real: ignoring the replacement policy.
distractor_kind.3.17: unweighted mean of letter grades. (a) no. (b) a different averaging rule, 3.17; inside (2, 4). Its direction depends on which grades sit on the heavy courses, which a solver cannot read without weighting. Lattice: 3.17 rounds from 76/24. (d) real: forgetting credit weights.
distractor_kind.3.25: both attempts' credits counted, both at the retake grade. (a) no. (b) inside (2, 4). Lattice: 3.25 = 78/24 exactly, so it survives a k/24 test. (d) real: misreading "replaced" as "the new grade overwrites the old one but both attempts stay on the transcript".

bounds: 2 < v < 4 (grades counted run from C to A)
mechanism: letter grade points A=4 B=3 C=2 D=1
arith_class_check: Checked the stem-readable lattice: counted credits are 24, so the key must round from k/24; every distractor also rounds from some k/24 (71/24, 76/24, 78/24), so the integrality test leaves all four. No other class property.
one_sided_check: Key largest; three different error kinds. The unweighted-mean error can go either way in general (it is below here only because the A grades sit on the 5-credit courses), so the stem does not reveal that the natural errors all lower the GPA.
interior_parity_check: Interior options 3.17 and 3.25: both 2-decimal values, 3 significant digits, equal display complexity; key 3.29 is the largest, not interior.

topic_tag: splitting a shared ride fare leg by leg among the riders aboard
subskill: pricing each leg of a multi-stop trip from a per-mile rate, dividing each leg among the riders present for it, and adding an equally shared base fee
prompt: Three coworkers share one ride-hail trip home. The fare is a $3.45 base fee plus $1.85 per mile. The car drives 6.2 miles to Ana's stop, then 4.6 more miles to Ben's stop, then 7.8 more miles to Cy's stop. They split the fare this way: the base fee is shared equally by all three, and the cost of each leg (the miles between consecutive stops) is shared equally by the riders who are in the car during that leg. To the nearest cent, how much does Cy pay?
explanation: Cy pays one third of the base fee, 3.45 ÷ 3 = $1.15. The first leg costs 6.2 × 1.85 = $11.47, shared by all three: $3.823. The second leg costs 4.6 × 1.85 = $8.51, shared by Ben and Cy: $4.255. The last leg costs 7.8 × 1.85 = $14.43, paid by Cy alone. Cy pays 1.15 + 3.823 + 4.255 + 14.43 ≈ $23.66. The option "22.24" splits the second leg three ways, as if Ana were still in the car. The option "19.78" splits the whole $37.86 fare in proportion to the miles each person rode (6.2, 10.8, and 18.6 miles). The option "18.93" splits the fare in proportion to the number of legs each person rode (1, 2, and 3).

distractor_solve.19.78: const b=3.45,r=1.85; const tot=b+r*(6.2+4.6+7.8); const pm=6.2+10.8+18.6; return (Math.round(18.6/pm*tot*100+1e-9)/100).toFixed(2);

distractor_kind.18.93: fare split by number of legs ridden (1:2:3). (a) no. (b) a different sharing rule, 18.93. Cheapest bound: Cy pays at least his solo last leg plus his base share, 14.43 + 1.15 = 15.58, and at most the whole fare 37.86; strictly inside. (d) real: "Cy rode three legs out of six rider-legs".
distractor_kind.19.78: fare split in proportion to miles ridden. (a) no. (b) 19.78, inside (15.58, 37.86). (d) real: the other common "fair" rule.
distractor_kind.22.24: second leg divided by three riders instead of two. (a) no parameter extreme: the stem fixes the riders on each leg. (b) 22.24, inside (15.58, 37.86). (d) real: losing track of who is still in the car after the first stop.

mechanism: cost of each leg shared by riders in the car
arith_class_check: No. Fares to the cent with nonzero last digits; Cy's share involves thirds and halves of cents, so no option is forced to any divisibility class.
one_sided_check: Key largest; three different error kinds (two different whole-fare sharing rules and a rider-count slip). Whether a whole-fare proportional rule charges Cy more or less than the leg rule is not visible without computing it, so the stem does not reveal that the natural errors all lower his share.
interior_parity_check: Interior options 19.78 and 22.24: both 2-decimal dollar amounts with nonzero cents, 4 significant digits; key 23.66 is the largest, not interior.

topic_tag: baseboard trim for a room measured on a scale drawing
subskill: scaling fractional drawing measurements to feet for both the walls and the doorway openings, removing the openings from the perimeter, and pricing by the linear foot
prompt: On a floor plan drawn to the scale 1/4 inch = 1 foot, a rectangular room is shown as 5 1/4 inches by 4 1/2 inches. Baseboard trim will run along every wall of the room except across its two doorways, which are 3/4 inch and 5/8 inch wide on the plan. Trim costs $2.87 per linear foot, and only the exact length needed is bought. To the nearest cent, what is the cost of the trim?
explanation: At 4 feet per inch of plan, the room is 5.25 × 4 = 21 ft by 4.5 × 4 = 18 ft, so the walls total 2(21 + 18) = 78 ft. The doorways are 0.75 × 4 = 3 ft and 0.625 × 4 = 2.5 ft, so the trim is 78 − 5.5 = 72.5 ft, costing 72.5 × 2.87 ≈ $208.08. The option "192.29" subtracts each doorway twice, once for each side of the opening (67 ft). The option "216.69" subtracts only the 2.5-foot doorway (75.5 ft). The option "219.91" subtracts the doorway widths in plan inches, 1 3/8, without scaling them to feet (76.625 ft).

distractor_kind.192.29: doorways subtracted twice. (a) no. (b) 67 ft x 2.87 = 192.29. Cheapest bracket over the cost: at most the full perimeter 78 ft (223.86) and at least 2 x longest side 42 ft (120.54); strictly inside. (d) real: treating each opening as two wall faces.
distractor_kind.216.69: one doorway forgotten. (a) no. (b) 216.69, inside (120.54, 223.86), not on the full-perimeter ceiling. (d) real.
distractor_kind.219.91: doorway widths left in plan inches. (a) no. (b) 219.91, inside; the ceiling 223.86 is 3.95 away. (d) real: scaling the room but not the openings.

219.91.error_kind: scale not applied to a part

arith_class_check: No. All four are 2.87 x (a length) rounded to cents with nonzero last digits; lengths 72.5, 67, 75.5, 76.625 give no shared or lone divisibility visible from the stem.

topic_tag: server tip-out computed partly on sales and partly on tips
subskill: applying percents to two different bases (sales and tips) and subtracting each share from the tips
prompt: At a restaurant, each server "tips out" to coworkers at the end of a shift: 3% of the server's food-and-drink SALES goes to the bussers, 1.5% of the server's SALES goes to the host, and 10% of the server's TIPS goes to the bartender. All three amounts are figured from the shift's totals and are paid out of the server's tips. During one shift, Mara had sales of $1,418.60 and received $247.35 in tips. To the nearest cent, how much of her tips does Mara keep after tipping out?
explanation: Bussers and host get 4.5% of sales: 0.045 × 1,418.60 = $63.837. The bartender gets 10% of tips: 0.10 × 247.35 = $24.735. Mara keeps 247.35 − 63.837 − 24.735 ≈ $158.78. The option "147.65" figures the bussers' and host's 4.5% on sales plus tips. The option "165.16" takes the bartender's 10% from what is left AFTER paying the bussers and host, instead of from her total tips. The option "211.48" figures the bussers' and host's shares on her tips instead of her sales.

distractor_kind.147.65: sales-based shares figured on sales plus tips. (a) no. (b) 147.65. Cheapest bracket over the amount kept: at most 90% of tips, 222.62 (bartender only), at least 0 ; finer, the sales shares are about 4.5% of about 1,400, near 64, so roughly 247 - 64 - 25 = 158 give or take a couple of dollars, which is the work itself. Strictly inside (0, 222.62). (d) real: blurring which total a percent is taken of.
distractor_kind.165.16: bartender share taken from the remainder. (a) no. (b) 165.16, inside. (d) real: applying percents in sequence when the stem says each is figured from the shift totals.
distractor_kind.211.48: sales-based shares figured on tips. (a) no. (b) 211.48, inside (0, 222.62); not on the 90%-of-tips ceiling. (d) real: reading "3% goes to the bussers" as 3% of the tips, which is the most common tip-out misreading.

mechanism: percent of sales to bussers and host

topic_tag: slugging percentage from hit types and at-bats

topic_tag: average speed needed for the remaining distance to meet a deadline
subskill: converting clock times and minutes to hours, subtracting time already used (driving and a stop), and dividing the remaining distance by the remaining time
prompt: Dae must drive 298 kilometers to arrive by 2:15 p.m. He leaves at 9:30 a.m. and drives the first 121 kilometers at an average speed of 84 kilometers per hour. The required speed is 177 ÷ 2.9762 ≈ 59.47 km/h. The option "56.92" writes the 20-minute stop as 0.20 hour. The option "62.74" is the average speed for the whole 298-km trip over 4.75 hours, not the speed needed for the rest. The option "66.14" writes 4 hours 45 minutes as 4.45 hours.

(b) neighbouring quantity (the average for the entire trip) = 62.74; it is not an endpoint of the feasible interval, since the required speed depends on how the first part went. The option "3514" charges 1,870 ÷ 250 = 7.48 pauses.
